The methodology involved developing a comprehensive SBC strategy with government partners, including the Ministry of Education and Skills Development, Ministry of Health, and Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock, and implementing SBC activities in 15 schools in Thimphu and Chhukha districts. Key findings indicate that while knowledge and awareness of healthy and unhealthy foods were relatively high, poor accessibility and affordability of healthy foods and abundant availability of inexpensive, convenient, and ultra-processed snacks were identified as determinants of poor-quality diets. The evaluation also highlights the effectiveness of edutainment as a medium for delivering nutrition education, as evidenced by the success of "Pinda's Magic Bowl," a nutrition education television programme that has been rebroadcast and uploaded onto YouTube channels. Implications of this evaluation suggest that targeted policy and programmatic tools and campaigns are necessary to address specific drivers and barriers to healthy eating, and that continued support for SBC initiatives is required to promote healthy diets among schoolchildren and adolescents in Bhutan.

This evaluation aimed to assess the impact of staple food inflation on the nutritional well-being of the Armenian population. Utilizing data from the Statistical Committee of RA, the study analyzed the dietary patterns of the population in various regions, with a focus on the proportion of individuals consuming 70% potato and bread. The findings indicate that the highest prevalence of this dietary pattern was observed in Armavir (30.1%), followed by Gegharkunik (25.4%) and Ararat (19.1%). The inflation of staple foods, such as bread and potatoes, may compromise the ability of these populations to maintain adequate nutrition and cover essential expenses, given their relatively low average nominal wages, which stood at AMD 297,624 in June 2025.

This evaluation aimed to assess the challenges and opportunities that promote and achieve digital financial inclusion in Belize, with a focus on the government's efforts to deliver social assistance benefits through digital payment solutions. The study employed a face-to-face survey of retailers and beneficiaries to capture their experiences and perceptions of digital payment modalities, as well as their demand- and supply-side dynamics within the ecosystem. Key findings include the diverse demographics and geographic disparities in Belize that influence access to and use of digital and financial services, with significant disparities in mobile phone ownership, internet access, and access to digital and financial services across different demographics and regions. The survey revealed that retailers face challenges in adopting and delivering financial services, including unfamiliarity with technology, high costs of operating POS machines, and limited number of participating merchants. Beneficiaries also reported challenges in accessing digital payment solutions, including limited access to agent locations in rural areas and insufficient assistance to cover monthly expenses. The study's findings have implications for the government's efforts to promote financial inclusion and improve the delivery of social assistance to its most vulnerable populations, highlighting the need for deeper insight into the challenges, opportunities, and behavioural dynamics of both beneficiaries and merchants to unlock the full potential of digital payments in Belize.

This evaluation aimed to assess the effectiveness of the World Food Programme's (WFP) Private Sector Partnerships and Fundraising (PSPF) Strategy, which was implemented from 2019 to 2022. The evaluation objective was to evaluate the progress made towards achieving the Strategy's objectives, identify areas for improvement, and provide recommendations for future development. The methodology involved a retrospective construction of a theory of change, development of a typology of private sector partnerships, in-depth reviews of internal and external documents, stakeholder interviews, a web-based survey of WFP country offices, and a review of nine partnership exemplars. Key findings included the growth of the Global Partnership team, PPF support functions, and regional partnership officers, as well as the establishment of new global partnerships and the expansion of existing ones. However, the evaluation also identified gaps in strategic direction for local level partnerships, a lack of awareness within WFP of the Strategy's implementation and achievements, and a need for more clarity on roles and responsibilities between PPF and other WFP teams. The evaluation recommended clarifying WFP's organizational direction and ambition for private sector partnerships, positioning private sector partnerships in the context of WFP's Executive Director priorities, and outlining the requirements for a successful global philanthropy programme. Additionally, the evaluation recommended renegotiating the Memorandum of Understanding with WFP USA, clarifying roles and responsibilities between WFP and WFP Friends organizations, and establishing transparent systems and processes for PSPF. The evaluation's implications suggest that WFP has immense potential to further grow its private sector engagement, provided it is willing to commit to and invest in this.

This evaluation aims to assess the effectiveness of the Environmental and Social Management Framework (ESMF) for the Myanmar Community Resilience Project, implemented by the World Food Programme (WFP) in collaboration with the World Bank. The evaluation objective is to ensure that the project's activities and benefits reach the most vulnerable and in-need households while minimizing environmental and social risks. The methodology involves a review of literature, consultations with WFP field teams and experts, and a review of field needs assessments, as well as relevant institutional and policy frameworks. The ESMF identifies potential environmental and social risks, including harm to human health and security, and outlines measures to avoid, minimize, and mitigate these risks. The framework also ensures compliance with Myanmar legislations, the World Bank's Environmental and Social Framework (ESF), and WFP's policies. Key findings include the implementation of E&S risk management measures as part of regular project monitoring, the provision of awareness raising and training to relevant stakeholders, and the tracking of grievances/community feedback during project implementation. The implications of this evaluation are that the ESMF provides a comprehensive framework for managing environmental and social risks, and that the World Bank's support will be crucial in ensuring the effective implementation of the ESMF.

This evaluation aimed to assess the environmental and social risks associated with the World Food Programme's (WFP) project in Myanmar, specifically the Community Resilience Project. The evaluation objective was to identify and mitigate potential risks to project workers, community members, and the environment. The methodology involved a review of literature, consultations with WFP field teams and experts, and a review of field needs assessments. Key findings included potential risks to project workers and community members, including health and safety risks, security risks, and social risks such as exclusion and discrimination. The evaluation also identified environmental risks, including solid waste management and food safety risks. To mitigate these risks, the WFP will implement measures such as regular monitoring, training for staff and volunteers, and awareness-raising activities for communities and contractors. The evaluation implications are that the WFP must ensure compliance with its policies and procedures, including the Environmental and Social Management Framework (ESMF), the Social and Environmental Policy (SEP), and the Environmental and Social Commitment Plan (ESCP). The WFP must also ensure that its grievance mechanism is accessible to disadvantaged and vulnerable groups and that it provides transparent information on project activities and benefits.

This evaluation aims to assess the effectiveness of the World Food Programme's (WFP) Stakeholder Engagement Plan (SEP) in ensuring free, prior, and informed consultation with ethnic minority communities in Myanmar, as required by the World Bank's Environmental and Social Standard 7. The evaluation methodology involves a review of the SEP, stakeholder engagement activities, and grievance mechanisms implemented by WFP and its cooperating partners (CPs). Key findings include the WFP's commitment to mainstreaming accountability to affected people across its operations, the establishment of a Community Engagement Mechanism (CEM) to provide information, engage beneficiaries, and receive feedback and complaints, and the use of culturally appropriate and gender-sensitive consultations with ethnic minority communities. The evaluation also highlights the importance of grievance mechanisms, such as the CEM, in resolving complaints and building trust with communities. The implications of this evaluation are that WFP and its CPs must continue to prioritize stakeholder engagement and grievance mechanisms to ensure the effective implementation of the project and the protection of vulnerable communities.

This evaluation aimed to assess the appropriateness of antenatal care recommendations for pregnant women. The methodology involved reviewing existing guidelines and expert consensus, specifically the 2012 recommendations from the French National Authority for Health (HAS) and a 2017 study. Key findings indicate that a low-dose approach is suggested when the viral load is decreasing, and that a scheduled cesarean delivery at term may be indicated in certain cases. The implications of these findings are that healthcare providers should consult the HAS website for up-to-date guidelines on antenatal care, and prioritize recommendations for future adult health, excluding iron and folic acid supplementation.

This impact evaluation aimed to assess the effectiveness of anticipatory humanitarian assistance (AA) in the form of unconditional cash transfers on agricultural outcomes, livelihood, migration, and other financial outcomes during the recovery period after a severe flood in Nepal. To achieve this objective, a clustered randomized controlled trial (RCT) was conducted in 140 villages, with 1,499 households receiving AA assistance and 1,484 households receiving traditional post-flood assistance. The evaluation collected quantitative follow-up panel data in three rounds and qualitative data in one round from approximately 2,300 households. The key findings indicate that AA transfers had a positive impact on food security, with households in the AA group experiencing significantly better food security immediately following the floods. However, these effects dissipated in the medium and long term, and no significant impacts were detected for key livelihood outcomes, such as agricultural outcomes and migration. Notably, households in the AA group were 15 percent less likely to engage in risky coping strategies, and they experienced a reduction in house repair expenses. The evaluation suggests that AA transfers can yield benefits in terms of food security and mitigating negative mental health impacts following climate disasters. However, the effectiveness of AA may vary depending on factors such as the severity of the flood, the speed of transfer disbursement, and the selection and prioritization of beneficiaries.

This evaluation aimed to assess the economic vulnerability of municipalities in Nepal to the COVID-19 pandemic, with a focus on identifying areas that require immediate attention and resource allocation. To achieve this objective, a comprehensive framework was developed, rooted in the conceptualization of vulnerability as a function of exposure, sensitivity, and adaptive capacity. The framework utilized a combination of indicators, including job loss, loss of income, and the prevalence of socially marginalized groups, to assess exposure and sensitivity. Adaptive capacity was evaluated through a range of factors, including access to basic services and remittance dependency. The resulting Economic Vulnerability Index (EVI) was used to rank municipalities across the country, with a focus on highlighting areas where both exposure and sensitivity are high, and adaptive capacity is low. Key findings indicate that vulnerability is concentrated in Karnali Province, Province 2, and Sudurpaschim Province, with notable municipalities in Province 1, Gandaki Province, and Province 5 classified among the most vulnerable. The EVI has been applied to target interventions, including food security programs, and has been used as a basis to prioritize more in-depth inquiries and data collection. The evaluation highlights the importance of considering multiple dimensions of vulnerability and the need for a consolidated approach to understanding economic vulnerability in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic.

This impact evaluation aimed to assess the effectiveness of the World Food Programme (WFP) resilience programme in improving food security and resilience capacities among households in targeted communities. To achieve this objective, a clustered randomized design was employed, where FFA sites and villages were assigned to either the WFP programme group or the control group. The evaluation used a sample of households that were classified as "very poor" and "poor" and were eligible for FFA and LSS, as well as households in primary villages closest to the FFA sites. The results showed that the programme had a positive impact on food security, particularly among the poorest households that were eligible for FFA and LSS. The programme increased the share of households with livestock and improved food security, with the largest impact observed during the first year of programme implementation. However, the impacts on food security were not sustained throughout the year, suggesting that increases in food production were not sufficient, or households did not develop other strategies to smooth the effects on food security. The evaluation also found that the programme increased collective action among households in programme communities, with members of more groups, spending more time volunteering in community activities, and working on community projects. The results have implications for the targeting of resilience programmes, suggesting that targeting "less poor" households with additional components may not be essential for contributing to food security and resilience capacities.

The evaluation objective of the UNICEF-WFP Partnership for Resilience and Social Cohesion in the Diffa Region was to assess the effectiveness of the partnership in enhancing community resilience and social cohesion in the region. The evaluation methodology involved a review of reports submitted to the German Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ) from May 2022 to April 2023, as well as interviews with community members and stakeholders.

Key findings of the evaluation indicate that the partnership has achieved significant results in strengthening community resilience and social cohesion. These include improved nutritional outcomes in households, enhanced community engagement and participation in decision-making, and strengthened capacities of local and regional authorities to provide social services and emergency preparedness. Additionally, the partnership has supported the development of inclusive institutional frameworks for the participation of youth and marginalized groups in decision-making, and has strengthened community capacities and engagement through community-based participatory planning and civic and social engagement activities.

The implications of these findings suggest that the UNICEF-WFP Partnership for Resilience and Social Cohesion in the Diffa Region has been effective in enhancing community resilience and social cohesion, and has contributed to improved livelihoods and youth employment opportunities, as well as increased access to social services and improved nutrition, health, and protection outcomes.

This evaluation aimed to assess the impact of food card assistance on the nutrition and food security of beneficiary households in Armenia. The study employed a mixed-methods approach, combining qualitative data from focus group discussions with quantitative data sources to enhance the credibility of the findings. Key findings indicate that food card holders face challenges in planning and budgeting for food purchases, particularly due to limited time and financial resources. The study also highlights the importance of parental influence over children's food choices, with many participants expressing a strong belief in the nutritional value of homemade and traditional dishes. However, awareness and education on healthy eating are limited, and participants often rely on social media, television, and neighbors for information on nutrition. The study also found that financial constraints, lack of time, and limited access to healthy food options hinder the ability of households to adopt healthy eating habits. The evaluation suggests that addressing these challenges through targeted interventions, such as nutrition education and awareness-raising campaigns, may help improve the nutrition and food security of beneficiary households.

This evaluation aimed to assess the impact of malnutrition on children under 5 and the effectiveness of World Food Programme (WFP) interventions in addressing this issue. The evaluation methodology involved analyzing data from WFP's 19 largest operations, as well as case studies from specific countries, including Chad and Yemen. Key findings indicate that 148 million children under 5 are chronically malnourished, 45 million are acutely malnourished, and 37 million are overweight, with micronutrient deficiencies affecting nearly half of preschool-aged children. Malnutrition is a leading driver of death and disease among young children, particularly in countries facing conflict, climate shocks, and economic crises. The evaluation also highlights the importance of addressing the root causes of food insecurity and malnutrition, including poverty, ineffective food systems, and recurrent humanitarian emergencies. Despite a global shortfall of over US$1 billion in funding for lifesaving nutrition programming, WFP has made significant progress in addressing malnutrition, including the distribution of specialized nutritious food (SNF) to prevent acute malnutrition. The evaluation's findings have implications for WFP's strategic plan, emphasizing the need to maximize the contribution to tackling malnutrition and improving diets globally.

This evaluation aimed to assess the effectiveness of the World Food Programme's (WFP) nutrition portfolio in Madagascar, as outlined in the Country Strategic Plan. The evaluation methodology involved an examination of WFP's cross-cutting nutrition initiatives, including school feeding and agricultural value chain programmes. Key findings indicate that WFP has made significant progress in strengthening institutional capacity for nutrition governance, improving access to nutritious diets, and enhancing access to prevention and treatment services for malnutrition. Specifically, the evaluation highlights the establishment of three semi-industrial and artisanal food processing units, the development of a nutritious menu catalogue, and the facilitation of cash transfers to diversify school meals. Additionally, WFP has developed a toolkit and training plan to promote healthy practices among students. The implications of these findings suggest that WFP's nutrition portfolio has contributed to reducing forms of malnutrition, improving dietary diversity, and promoting better child feeding and care practices in Madagascar.

The evaluation objective of the Emergency Social Protection and Jobs COVID-19 Response Parent Project in the West Bank and Gaza is to ensure the effective implementation of environmental and social safeguards, in accordance with the Environmental and Social Standards (ESSs) and the Environmental and Social Commitment Plan (ESCP). The methodology employed involves the maintenance of an Environment and Social Officer (ESO) by the Ministry of Finance (MoF) and the hiring of a qualified Environmental and Social Specialist by the World Food Programme (WFP) to support the management of environmental and social risks and impacts. The key findings of the evaluation include the implementation of the ESMF and SFA, the conduct of social assessments and reviews, and the maintenance of a grievance mechanism. The implications of these findings are that the project is well-positioned to address environmental and social risks and impacts, and that the WFP's existing grievance mechanisms will be used to facilitate the resolution of concerns and grievances related to the project.

The evaluation objective of this Stakeholder Engagement Plan (SEP) is to assess the effectiveness of stakeholder engagement mechanisms in ensuring informed participation and feedback throughout the project cycle. The methodology employed involves conducting consultation workshops with relevant stakeholders, providing clear guidance on complaints handling through the grievance mechanism (GM), and documenting stakeholder engagement activities as part of project progress reporting requirements. Key findings include the successful implementation of consultation workshops, the establishment of a grievance mechanism to resolve complaints and grievances in a timely and effective manner, and the provision of clear information on stakeholder engagement activities and grievance mechanisms to all project stakeholders. The implications of these findings suggest that the SEP has been effective in promoting stakeholder engagement and ensuring that project activities are responsive to stakeholder needs and concerns.

This evaluation aimed to assess the effectiveness of the World Food Programme's (WFP) Inclusive Risk Financing (IRF) programmes in mitigating the impacts of climate-related shocks on vulnerable communities. The evaluation employed a mixed-methods approach, combining quantitative data on insurance payouts and beneficiary numbers with qualitative insights from programme implementation and beneficiary experiences. Key findings indicate that the IRF programmes have provided a critical lifeline to communities threatened by climate shocks, with notable successes in Ethiopia's Somali region, where US$41.5 million in insurance payouts benefited almost 1.5 million people. The evaluation also highlights the strategic value of the Trust Fund modality in securing flexible, long-term investments and enabling the introduction of innovative solutions tailored to local risk profiles. The scale-up of WFP's IRF portfolio was made possible through multi-year financial support from long-term donor partners. The implications of this evaluation are that continued investment in the IRF programmes is essential to build a sustainable and resilient future for millions of people facing the brunt of the climate crisis.

This evaluation aimed to assess the effectiveness of the World Food Programme's (WFP) disaster risk financing (DRF) solutions in reducing the protection gap for vulnerable populations. The evaluation methodology involved an analysis of WFP's DRF portfolio, including its risk layering approach, contingency fund, and Catastrophe Layer, as well as its partnerships with governments and organizations such as the African Union's African Risk Capacity (ARC) and the Caribbean Catastrophe Risk Insurance Facility (CCRIF). Key findings include the successful implementation of a risk layering strategy in Mali, which effectively addressed different levels of risks, and the timely disbursement of funds following Hurricane Beryl in 2024, enabling WFP to provide critical food assistance to affected populations. Additionally, the evaluation highlighted the importance of inclusive risk financing, as seen in the record US$868,345 insurance payout to 61,943 affected farmers in Ethiopia in 2024. The implications of these findings suggest that WFP's DRF solutions can contribute to reducing the protection gap and ensuring sustainability in the mid and long term through close government involvement and integration with adaptive social protection systems.

This study aimed to evaluate the current school meal supply chain in Sub-Saharan Africa, with a focus on identifying practices that influence the impact of school feeding programs on planetary health. To achieve this objective, a round of stakeholder consultations was conducted from May 9th to June 16th, 2024, to understand the status and approaches used in school meal procurement to mitigate the environmental impact of the food supply chain. The key findings of this study highlight the need for a more comprehensive approach to school meal procurement, considering not only environmental impacts but also social and economic benefits. Specifically, the study emphasizes the importance of integrating locally sourced food into school meals, adopting sustainable agricultural practices, and promoting ecologically sustainable food systems. The proposed evaluation tool can serve as a starting point to engage with parents and farmers on criteria for food production and sourcing, potentially catalysing a shift toward sustainability. The implications of this study suggest that sustainable procurement practices that consider both social and environmental impacts along the food supply chain will enhance local markets, driving economic equity while ensuring long-term sustainability and healthy diets for school-going children.

This evaluation aims to assess the potential of solar e-cooking solutions in displacement settings to contribute to global climate change mitigation efforts and sustainable development. The study employed a qualitative methodology, analyzing existing literature and case studies to identify key challenges and opportunities for scaling up solar e-cooking technologies. The evaluation found that international carbon markets, including Article 6 of the Paris Agreement and voluntary carbon markets, have the potential to generate carbon finance that promotes sustainable cooking practices. However, barriers to uptake remain, including high costs of clean cooking and electricity access technologies, limited private sector engagement in remote areas, and variable quality of energy technologies. The study also identified opportunities for growth, including the potential for solar e-cooking to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, enhance resilience to climate shocks, and preserve natural resources. The evaluation recommends activating the supply of solar e-cooking technologies, raising awareness of the benefits of such cooking technologies, and providing financing options for households to purchase solar e-cooking systems. Furthermore, the study suggests that mainstreaming renewable-powered e-cooking technologies can help countries secure large flows of concessional climate finance and elevate the prominence of e-cooking targets and investment strategies in their sustainable development agendas.

This evaluation aimed to assess the effectiveness of pre-arranged finance (PAF) in enhancing food security and reducing the impacts of predictable shocks, particularly in the context of the escalating climate crisis. The evaluation employed a qualitative methodology, drawing on existing literature and case studies, to examine the integration of PAF instruments in humanitarian programming. Key findings indicate that PAF has the potential to shift from costly reactive approaches to efficient proactive support, with only 2 percent of international crisis finance currently pre-arranged. The World Food Programme (WFP) aims to increase PAF tenfold by 2035, making it the default crisis financing approach for predictable and modellable risks. Case studies, such as Anticipatory Actions (AA) and Disaster Risk Financing (DRF), demonstrate the effectiveness of PAF in strengthening resilience, providing financial protection, and helping communities adapt to climate-related shocks. The evaluation highlights the importance of increasing pre-arranged finance to provide assistance more effectively and maximize every dollar spent, particularly in the face of escalating food insecurity, poverty, and climate-related threats.

This evaluation aims to assess the effectiveness of the World Food Programme's (WFP) Gender-Based Violence (GBV), Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (SEA), and Sexual Harassment (SH) Action Plan in mitigating risks and promoting a safe and respectful work environment. The evaluation methodology involves an analysis of existing policies, training programs, and community awareness initiatives. Key findings indicate that WFP has a zero-tolerance policy on SEA, with a robust reporting mechanism and a reliable countrywide Grievance Redressal Mechanism (GRM) system in place. However, the increasing risk of service providers being targeted, particularly women-led organizations, necessitates the implementation of targeted prevention measures. The evaluation highlights the importance of regular SEA risk assessments, awareness sessions for staff, volunteers, and community members, and the establishment of safe referral pathways for survivors of GBV/SEA. The implications of these findings suggest that WFP should prioritize the integration of SEA/SH into its GRM systems, collaborate with key PSEA and GBV actors, and ensure the safe referral of survivors to appropriate service providers.

This evaluation aimed to assess the impact of economic and climatic factors on food prices in the Kyrgyz Republic. The methodology involved analyzing operational daily food price data collected by the National Statistics Committee from 18 markets across the country, disaggregated at province level. Key findings indicate that the country's GDP growth is driven by goods-producing industries, services, and food taxes, but consumer price growth has been witnessed in all regions except Jalal-Abad and Chuy provinces. The prices of fuel and lubricants have increased by 10 percent, leading to higher transportation costs and affecting all other prices. Rising food and fuel prices, combined with inflation, have eroded the purchasing power of the most vulnerable populations, making it difficult for them to access a nutritious diet. The country's high import dependency on vegetable oil, wheat, and other basic food commodities due to low internal production and capacity for processing oil seeds has also been identified. The evaluation highlights the importance of currency movements as a driving force of retail prices of imported basic food commodities. Implications of these findings suggest that the Kyrgyz Republic needs to address its high import dependency and develop strategies to increase domestic production and processing capacity to ensure food security and stability in the face of volatile global oil markets.

This evaluation aimed to assess the effectiveness of the integrated risk management strategies implemented under the R4 initiative in strengthening farmers' food and income security. The evaluation employed a mixed-methods approach, combining quantitative and qualitative data from various sources, including surveys, meetings, and training sessions. Key findings indicate that the initiative has successfully reached a significant number of farmers, with 67,015 farmers (41 percent women) insured for the 2020 agricultural season in Amhara and Tigray regions. Additionally, 544 savings groups were established, with a cumulative savings of US$110,610 (ZMW 2,212,205) among 12,246 farmers (59 percent women). The initiative also promoted Conservation Agriculture (CA) techniques, with 17,835 farmers applying CA techniques, and 8,966 farmers trained in CA land preparation. Furthermore, 2,000 farmers (96 percent women) accessed flood index insurance, with a total payout sum of US$63,793 (Taka 54,000,000). The evaluation's implications suggest that the integrated risk management approach has the potential to improve farmers' resilience to climate-related shocks and stressors, and that the initiative's components, including risk transfer, risk reduction, and risk reserves, are critical in achieving this goal.

The evaluation objective of the 2nd Steering Committee Meeting of the RBA/Canada resilience initiative was to discuss the implementation of the partnership, take stock of preliminary results, and identify areas for improvement and further support. The meeting was conducted in Niger between September 16th and 20th, 2019, and involved participants from Canada and RBA representation from Niger, DRC, Somalia, and HQ. The methodology employed included a field visit to RBA Niger project sites in Maradi and Zinder, a one-day meeting in Niamey, and discussions on implementation, preliminary results, and follow-up opportunities. Key findings included the need to strengthen support for M&E, align reporting systems, and streamline the process of receiving funds for project implementation. Additionally, there was a need to define clear, common messages on the RBA Canada initiative, scale up knowledge management, and clarify IFAD's financing. The implications of these findings include the potential to improve the effectiveness and efficiency of the RBA/Canada initiative, enhance collaboration with UNICEF, and strengthen rural finance and village savings and loans associations in Niger. Overall, the meeting provided an opportunity for countries to share experiences and learning, identify areas for improvement, and plan for the future of the initiative.

This evaluation aimed to analyze patterns of food insecurity and malnutrition in Rajasthan, identify the most affected areas and population groups, and the underlying factors contributing to their vulnerability. The study employed a comprehensive methodology, utilizing various secondary sources such as Census 2011, National Family Health Surveys (NFHS 3, 4, and 5), Consumer Expenditure Surveys (CES), and administrative data from government departments. Key findings indicate that rural regions in Rajasthan have higher rates of stunting and underweight among children under five, while urban areas show slightly higher rates of wasting and overweight/obesity. The analysis also reveals that the bottom 25 percent population in Rajasthan has higher energy, protein, and fat intake compared to their national counterparts. Furthermore, the study found that Rajasthan has made significant strides in reducing child undernutrition and mortality, particularly among the Empowered Action Group (EAG) states, between 2015-16 and 2019-21. The evaluation highlights the need for continued analysis and attention to address the underlying factors contributing to food and nutrition insecurity in Rajasthan, particularly in districts with high proportions of agriculture labourers and vulnerable populations. The findings have implications for policymakers and stakeholders to develop targeted interventions and strategies to improve food and nutrition security in the state.

This report aims to evaluate the extent to which countries have implemented school health and nutrition (SHN) policies and programmes, with a focus on the core components of SHN, including education for health and well-being, the school physical environment, the school socioemotional environment, school health services, and school feeding programmes. The evaluation draws on available data and case study examples to provide an overview of the extent to which countries are implementing SHN programmes and considers available evidence about implementation of each core component. The findings show that SHN programmes are one of the most widely implemented public policies across the world, with many countries implementing activities in schools to promote the health, nutrition, and well-being of students. However, despite the conceptual shift towards a more holistic and integrated approach, many countries have yet to develop or implement comprehensive school health policies and programmes. The analysis highlights the increasing priority that governments place on SHN and its role in achieving education sector goals, with around two-thirds of countries having national standards on health-promoting schools. The report also highlights the need for a whole-school approach to address student health and well-being, with few national policies taking a comprehensive or whole-school approach. The evaluation objective is to assess the status of SHN policies and programmes globally, with a focus on the core components of SHN. The methodology involves drawing on available data and case study examples to provide an overview of the extent to which countries are implementing SHN programmes. The key findings include the widespread implementation of SHN programmes, the increasing priority placed on SHN by governments, and the need for a whole-school approach to address student health and well-being. The implications of the findings are that governments and development partners should prioritize the development and implementation of comprehensive school health policies and programmes, and that a whole-school approach is necessary to address student health and well-being.

This evaluation aimed to assess the effectiveness of Food Assistance for Assets (FFA) programmes in improving long-term food security and resilience of vulnerable communities in fragile contexts. The evaluation employed a mixed-methods approach, combining quantitative data from a 2024 cost-benefit analysis conducted by the United Nations University Institute for Environment and Human Security (UNU-EHS) in Niger with qualitative insights from community-oriented efforts. Key findings indicate that FFA activities can contribute to ecosystem restoration, with 2/3 of implemented assets showing improvements in vegetation and soil conditions. Furthermore, investing in land restoration measures for resilience and climate adaptation was found to be 3.3 to 3.5 times more cost-efficient than providing humanitarian aid for food insecure populations until 2055. The evaluation also highlights the importance of community-led initiatives, including the rehabilitation of over 13,400 ha of degraded lands, development of 2,300 ha of vegetable gardens, and training of 14,300 lead farmers in various technologies and practices. The implications of these findings suggest that FFA programmes can be a critical component of integrated resilience approaches and climate change adaptation strategies, particularly when implemented in a community-oriented and gender-transformative manner.

This evaluation aimed to assess the progress and outcomes of humanitarian programs implemented in various countries, including Kenya and Djibouti, with a focus on program sustainability and transition to government ownership. The evaluation methodology involved an analysis of Annual Country Reports and macroeconomic data sourced from government websites and official reports. Key findings indicate that, as of 2024, programs in Kenya and Djibouti have been successfully transitioned to government ownership, marking a significant milestone in program sustainability. Notably, Sudan's program indicators were waived for the 2024 reporting period, suggesting a need for further evaluation and support. The implications of these findings underscore the importance of effective program transition and government ownership in ensuring long-term sustainability and impact of humanitarian interventions.

This evaluation aimed to assess the effectiveness of the World Food Programme's (WFP) efforts in promoting resilient food systems, particularly in addressing climate change and improving food security, nutrition, and livelihoods. The evaluation methodology involved an analysis of WFP's programme portfolio, including its Smallholder Agricultural Market Support programme, and its engagement with Food Systems Coalitions and the Task Force. Key findings indicate that WFP's initiatives have the potential to enhance food security, improve nutrition, and support livelihoods, while also contributing to environmental sustainability. The evaluation highlights WFP's efforts to promote planet-friendly, diversified, and localized food production, as well as its value chain development approach aimed at improving the livelihoods of smallholder farmers. The implications of this evaluation suggest that WFP's approach to resilient food systems can have a positive impact on addressing climate change and improving food security outcomes, particularly in fragile and conflict-affected settings.

This evaluation aimed to assess the effectiveness of the World Food Programme's (WFP) revised Country Strategic Note (CRF) in measuring programme performance and contributing to the achievement of Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The evaluation methodology involved the development of indicators and metrics to measure the programme results chain, impact pathways, and strategic outcomes. The revised CRF is based on a hierarchy of measurable results, ensuring alignment with global and national development goals. Key findings include the alignment of strategic outcome, output, and activity categories with the new country portfolio budget structure, enabling WFP to view and analyse performance information and expenditure data. The evaluation also found that the revised CRF promotes the alignment of resources to results as a performance principle, key to transparency and accountability. The implications of this evaluation are that WFP will need to accommodate changing SDG indicators and incorporate new learning regarding programme and management performance in the coming years. The revised CRF will enable country offices to select indicators most relevant to the design and desired results of an intervention, rather than by strategic outcome category, allowing for more effective monitoring and reporting of programme performance.

This evaluation aimed to assess the impact of women's participation in FFA (working outside the household and receiving cash in return) on their social and economic empowerment. The analysis compared the FFA for women group to the comparison group, which was not targeted for programme participation. The evaluation employed a treatment-on-the-treated (ToT) analysis to estimate the impacts of women's participation in FFA. Key findings include modest improvements in food security and household consumption, particularly in the FFA for women group. However, household participation rates were significantly lower in the FFA for women arm, leading to reduced WFP cash support. Additionally, women's decision-making authority (agency) over consumption was negatively affected in both the FFA and FFA for women groups. The evaluation's findings suggest that targeting women with FFA may have mixed effects on their social and economic empowerment, with both positive and negative outcomes. The results have implications for programme design and implementation, highlighting the need to consider the potential trade-offs between different programme components and the importance of addressing the root causes of gender inequality.

This evaluation aimed to assess the relevance of the FY24 McGovern-Dole project design in contributing to a sustainable and effective implementation of the National School Feeding Programme (NSFP) in Rwanda, considering the government's readiness and capacities to manage the programme. The study employed a combination of methods, including situational assessment, desk review, and semi-structured key informant interviews, to gather data from various sources, including WFP and partner reports, government documents, and stakeholder interviews. The evaluation found that the FY24 project design is highly relevant in responding to gaps identified during the FY20 midterm evaluation, particularly in ensuring adequate support for and sustainability of the NSFP. The project's focus on policy coherence, advocacy, and capacity building aligns with the World Bank's SABER framework and the Government's priorities. The evaluation also identified early signs of systemic improvements in the NSFP, including increased government capacity, improved school meal quality, and enhanced smallholder engagement. However, the study also highlighted capacity constraints relevant to the NSFP, including procurement and sustainability pressures, gaps in monitoring and evaluation systems, and technical capacity gaps in some areas. The evaluation's findings will inform operational and strategic decision-making related to school feeding in Rwanda, contributing to the strengthening of national systems for school feeding, including planning, delivery, and monitoring capacities.

This evaluation aimed to assess the extent to which the Mastercard Foundation-funded "Strengthening food systems to empower smallholder farmers and young people" project, locally known as Shora Neza, addresses the needs and priorities of agri-entrepreneurs and smallholder farmers, especially youth and women, in Rwanda. Utilizing a mixed-methods approach, including a cross-sectional study design, desk review, surveys, key informant interviews, and focus group discussions, the evaluation collected primary data from programme participants, internal and external stakeholders, and programme documents. The findings indicate that the programme's strategic design, objectives, and implementation are addressing the needs and priorities of agri-preneurs and smallholder farmers, particularly youth and women, to a significant extent. The programme has successfully linked agri-entrepreneurs and smallholder farmers, especially women and youth, to formal food systems, and has empowered them with knowledge, skills, and resources to drive lasting change. The evaluation also found that the programme has considered the specific needs and barriers faced by women and young people within Rwanda's agricultural sector, and has laid the groundwork for continued impact beyond its lifespan. The results of this evaluation will inform how to serve beneficiaries more efficiently and effectively, and will contribute to the development of inclusive national food systems in Rwanda.

This evaluation aimed to assess the effectiveness of the Rural Rapid Transformation (RRT) Initiative in strengthening the resilience of vulnerable rural communities in southern Madagascar. The evaluation methodology involved monitoring the implementation of 11 RRT sites established since January 2023, with a focus on the integration of multifunctional solar platforms powering essential services, including access to clean water, digitalization, improved food storage and processing, climate-resilient agriculture, and social cohesion. Key findings from the evaluation included the successful establishment of RRT platforms as catalysts for local economic development, food security, and nutrition, with access to clean drinking water being the most significant benefit for communities. Other substantial benefits were identified in the areas of health, environmental impact, access to education, and economic empowerment. The evaluation also highlighted the need to adapt the size of energy kits to local needs, strengthen community capacities for management and long-term sustainability, and promote viable business models based on the sale of services. The RRT Initiative's management models, including community-based management, public-private partnerships, and private sector management, are being tailored to local contexts, with a sustainable business model currently being developed to integrate the sale of services.

This evaluation aimed to assess the effectiveness of the Home-Grown School Feeding (HGSF) model in Madagascar, implemented by the World Food Programme (WFP) in collaboration with the Government of Madagascar. The evaluation objective was to evaluate the progress and impact of the HGSF model in improving school nutrition and education outcomes. The methodology involved an analysis of programme data, including school enrolment rates, meal fortification, nutrition education activities, and procurement of commodities from smallholder farmers. Key findings indicate that, despite high primary school enrolment rates, only half of school children complete primary school on time. However, the HGSF model has shown promising results, with the procurement of 5,432 MT of commodities from smallholder farmers in 2024, and the expansion of HGSF coverage to 191 schools under the Mionjo project. The implications of these findings suggest that scaling up the HGSF model through capacity building, financial support, and increased coverage of schools is crucial to improving school nutrition and education outcomes in Madagascar.

This evaluation aimed to assess the effectiveness of nutrition and physical activity practices in promoting healthy eating habits and immune system strengthening among family members. The study employed a qualitative methodology, gathering information through representative sentences that highlighted the importance of consuming a balanced diet, limiting sugar, salt, and fat intake, and engaging in regular physical activities. Key findings revealed that a variety of safe and nutritionally balanced foods, including fruits and vegetables, are essential for strengthening the immune system and reducing the risk of disease. Moreover, cooking meals at home using clean tools and ingredients, and refraining from using excessive frying oil or artificial flavorings, can support children's immune systems and provide adequate energy. The study also emphasized the significance of breakfast in providing energy for daily activities and the importance of proper food handling and cooking practices to ensure food safety. The implications of these findings suggest that promoting healthy eating habits and physical activity practices can have a positive impact on immune system strengthening and disease prevention, highlighting the need for education and awareness-raising initiatives to support families in adopting these practices.

This evaluation aimed to assess the climate and weather conditions in the country from September to December 2025. The methodology involved analyzing remote sensing data, including land surface temperatures (LST), water levels, and Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) values. Key findings indicate that land surface temperatures were generally below average in September, while water levels in the Tonle Sap Lake and River remained close to the long-term average, albeit with a total lake volume 8.8% below its average. Vegetation conditions nationwide were slightly below the long-term average, with healthy vegetation observed in certain areas, but approximately 20,623 hectares of agricultural land were impacted by floods. The evaluation also suggests that rainfall patterns in December 2025 and January 2026 are expected to be near normal, with potential localized temperature fluctuations in October. The implications of these findings highlight the need for continued monitoring of climate and weather conditions to inform agricultural and humanitarian planning.

The evaluation objective was to assess the impact of the ongoing conflict on Lebanon's southern borders on the World Food Programme's (WFP) assistance delivery to affected populations. The evaluation employed a descriptive methodology, analyzing data on the number of people killed and displaced, assistance provided, and distribution site operations. Key findings indicate that the conflict resulted in 306 deaths, 90,000 displaced individuals, and 112,200 people assisted with emergency assistance. However, the conflict also led to the closure of three food distribution points, resulting in a 5% lower show-rate at distribution sites. To mitigate this impact, WFP identified and utilized alternative distribution points, and implemented a no-show distribution to reach more people. The evaluation also highlights the flexibility of the cash modality, which allowed beneficiaries to redeem their entitlements with minimal impact. The findings suggest a trend of households seeking safer zones further north, with a noticeable increase in redemption rates beyond 26 km. The evaluation's implications are that WFP's assistance delivery was adapted to respond to the evolving conflict situation, and that the cash modality provided flexibility in the face of operational challenges.

This evaluation aimed to assess the effectiveness of the United Nations World Food Programme's (WFP) security management system in Sudan. The evaluation methodology involved an examination of WFP's security plans, policies, and guidelines, as well as an analysis of the responsibilities and accountabilities of WFP officials and personnel. Key findings indicate that WFP's security management system is aligned with the United Nations Security Management System (UNSMS) policies and guidelines, and that the Country Director has overall responsibility for the security of WFP staff, supported by a team of security field officers. Furthermore, WFP ensures that cooperating partners and financial service providers operating within the framework of the World Bank's Environment and Social Framework. The evaluation also highlights the collaboration between WFP and other agencies to share insights on security risks and mitigation measures. The implications of these findings suggest the need for continued adherence to UNSMS policies and guidelines to ensure the safety and security of WFP personnel and operations in Sudan.

This evaluation aimed to assess the relevance, effectiveness, efficiency, impact, consistency, gender equity, country ownership, innovation, sustainability, replicability, scalability, and positive and negative unintended outcomes of the R4 project in Senegal. The project employed a consultative approach, bringing together information on food security trends, shocks, livelihoods, and seasonality at national, regional, and community levels. The evaluation methodology involved interviews with stakeholders, including direct beneficiaries, the WFP Country Office, cooperating partners, national and local authorities, and aid actors.

Key findings indicate that the project is well aligned with national priorities and strategies in terms of food and nutritional security, adaptation to climate change, territorialisation of public policies, gender equality, social protection, and financial inclusion. The project has demonstrated its relevance to the commitments made by the State, with plans to extend the R4 programme to scale up a flagship rural resilience programme combining four risk management strategies. The project has contributed to strengthening the productive capacity of communities, promoting community participatory approaches, securing food production through agricultural insurance, and improving women's and children's access to community care.

The evaluation also highlights the project's potential for scaling up, with activities such as climate information, village cereal banks, and savings and credit groups easily replicable at no or low additional cost. However, the project faced challenges in terms of capitalisation and communication, which hindered the authorities, aid actors, and the general public from being sufficiently informed about the project's actions, results, and best practices. The evaluation recommends improving the project's monitoring and evaluation framework, including the development of clear qualitative and quantitative indicators to measure its impacts.

The project's impact on social cohesion, food security, and climate resilience is evident, with communities unanimously pointing to these effects as beneficial in strengthening their climate resilience. The project's alignment with government, GCF, and WFP policies and strategies is also noted, with the R4 project contributing to the achievement of the NDC commitments. Overall

This evaluation aimed to assess the humanitarian needs of populations affected by widespread flooding, landslides, and lahar in the provinces of Albay, Catanduanes, and Camarines Sur. The assessment team visited 10 areas in these provinces, including evacuation centres and communities with limited access to basic needs such as food, water, and medicines. Key findings indicate that food and water remain top priority needs for affected populations, particularly those in evacuation centres and communities with disrupted access to regular supplies. The assessment also highlighted the challenges in distributing relief packs due to inaccessibility of some affected areas. Furthermore, the evaluation revealed that affected families will face long-term challenges, including damage to livelihoods and price increases of goods. To address these needs, it is recommended to leverage shock-responsive social protection programmes and utilize pre-existing lists of vulnerable households in the most affected areas.

This evaluation aimed to assess the viability of solar-powered Electric Pressure Cookers (EPCs) in improving food security and reducing malnutrition in vulnerable and food-insecure areas of Burkina Faso. The project, launched in 2025, introduced EPCs in ten school canteens across the Plateau Central, Nord, and Boucle du Mouhoun regions, equipped with solar photovoltaic systems, batteries, and essential control and protection systems. The methodology involved training cooks, school staff, and members of School Management Committees on efficient use of the appliances, as well as an internal early-stage site visit to observe the technology's performance, effectiveness, and potential challenges. Key findings indicate that EPCs were able to suitably cook all dishes, demonstrating versatility in accommodating local culinary practices, and allowing for more homogenous cooking and reduced food waste. However, maintenance of batteries and cleaning of solar panels were not performed regularly, and access to reliable and clean water supply was identified as a concern in several schools. Despite these challenges, the initiative has shown positive trends in improving school attendance, and has sparked curiosity among cooks, teachers, and the wider community. Implications suggest that regular maintenance and upkeep are crucial to ensure the optimal performance and long-term efficiency of the solar-powered EPC systems, and that access to reliable and clean water supply is essential for maintaining proper hygiene in kitchen operations.

This evaluation aimed to assess the effectiveness of Electric Pressure Cookers (EPCs) in reducing energy demand and improving cooking outcomes in schools in Lesotho. The study employed a mixed-methods approach, combining data collection through electric meters, cooking diaries, and interviews with cooks and school management. The evaluation found that EPCs significantly reduced energy demand, were a clean alternative to traditional cooking methods, and were compatible with existing power generation infrastructure. Key findings included a cost savings of approximately one third compared to LPG and one sixth compared to wood fuel, as well as improved cooking outcomes, including reduced food contamination and faster cooking times. The evaluation also highlighted the potential for EPCs to improve the efficiency of cooking and reduce the time required for cooking and washing. Overall, the study suggests that EPCs can be a viable and cost-effective solution for improving cooking outcomes in schools in Lesotho.

This evaluation aimed to assess the effectiveness of the World Food Programme's (WFP) Sustainable Livelihoods Opportunities (SLO) programme in promoting food security and economic mobility among marginalized communities. To achieve this objective, the evaluation employed a mixed-methods approach, combining quantitative data from programme implementation and monitoring with qualitative insights from key stakeholders. Key findings indicate that since 2020, the SLO programme has supported nearly 3 million people across 32 countries, with significant upskilling of almost 800,000 individuals and direct training of over 341,000 people. Moreover, in 2024, the programme reached 800,000 people with food assistance, with 54% being women and 32% forcibly displaced individuals. The evaluation highlights the programme's twofold approach, investing in corporate technical capacity and strengthening the role of key partners, including national authorities, civil society, and the local private sector. The findings suggest that doubling down on efforts to implement market-driven upskilling programmes and economic self-reliance actions can lower the need for recurrent humanitarian interventions, particularly in the context of climate change. By 2030, the programme aims to improve food security for 6 million people, enhance job/business skills for 2 million people, and provide access to self- or wage-employment for 1 million people. The evaluation emphasizes the importance of integrated and long-term programming, multi-year layering and sequencing of emergency assistance, transition programming, and livelihood development actions.

This evaluation aimed to assess the potential impact and risks of the proposed SANAD project activities on Project Affected Peoples in the project area, with a particular focus on effects on Indigenous Peoples/Sub-Saharan African Historically Underserved Traditional Local Communities (SSAHUTLC), vulnerable, and disadvantaged groups. The evaluation employed a social assessment methodology, including rapid assessments and community consultations, to understand the constraints on stakeholder engagement for vulnerable/disadvantaged groups, including indigenous/SSAHUTLC. Key findings revealed significant levels of financial exclusion in Kassala, West Darfur, and White Nile states, with particularly high levels of exclusion among women, rural populations, and nomads. The evaluation also highlighted the importance of addressing the risk of exclusion of SSAHUTLC, ethnic minorities, and vulnerable groups, and ensuring that project activities account for and are inclusive of their needs and aspirations. The implications of these findings suggest the need for deliberate efforts to economically empower women, address land grabbing and displacement, and promote financial inclusion, particularly among vulnerable populations.

This evaluation aimed to assess the effectiveness of the Social and Behavior Change Communication (SBCC) strategy implemented by the GTNS Project in promoting health and nutrition behaviors among community members. The evaluation employed a convenience sampling method, surveying eligible beneficiaries who had consented to being interviewed. The study collected pre- and post-test data to assess changes in knowledge, intention, and behavior related to health and nutrition practices. Key findings indicate that after completing the SBCC topic area, 75% of households recalled 3 key S&H messages, 66% intended to adopt practices that prevent illness, and 66% were confident in practicing handwashing with soap. Additionally, 66% of households intended to treat their water before consumption, and 50% of men and women attempted to make recipes from cooking demonstrations. These results suggest that the SBCC strategy was effective in increasing knowledge, intention, and behavior related to health and nutrition practices among community members. The implications of these findings are that the GTNS Project's SBCC strategy can be a valuable tool in promoting health and nutrition behaviors among community members, and that further scaling up of this strategy could lead to improved health outcomes.

This evaluation aimed to assess the effectiveness of age- and gender-sensitive social protection provisions in mitigating the impact of HIV/AIDS on human capital development, particularly among vulnerable adolescents and young people in sub-Saharan Africa. The evaluation employed a mixed-methods approach, combining literature reviews, program assessments, and stakeholder engagement to identify key findings and implications. The results indicate that targeted social protection provisions, including cash transfer programs, food assistance, and nutrition support, can effectively address the multiple deprivations affecting vulnerable adolescents and young people, including those living with HIV. These interventions have been shown to improve financial stability, school enrollment, and cognitive development outcomes, while also reducing the risk of new HIV infections. Furthermore, integrated prevention and mitigation measures, such as psychosocial support and adolescent-friendly clinics, can help tackle the drivers of new infections and mitigate the negative impacts of mortality and HIV-related morbidity on households. The evaluation highlights the importance of understanding contextual HIV risks, vulnerabilities, and age-specific needs of adolescents, particularly adolescent girls and young women, to enhance social protection interventions. Recommendations include ensuring that social protection investments respond to the most vulnerable adolescents and youth affected by HIV and AIDS, identifying barriers to accessing social protection programs, and engaging with young people in program design, implementation, and monitoring.

This evaluation aimed to assess the effectiveness of South-South and Triangular Cooperation (SSTC) initiatives in promoting sustainable agricultural development, food security, and nutrition in Africa. The evaluation methodology involved a comprehensive review of existing literature, case studies, and stakeholder engagement with key partners, including the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the World Food Programme (WFP), and the African Union. Key findings indicate that SSTC initiatives have contributed to enhancing food security, improving agricultural productivity, and addressing the root causes of hunger and malnutrition in Africa. Specifically, initiatives such as the China-Africa Agricultural Cooperation and Technical Innovation Alliance (CAASTIA), the China-Africa Rice Value Chain Initiative, and the School Feeding Coalition have demonstrated positive impacts on agricultural production, poverty reduction, and community development, particularly for vulnerable groups such as women and smallholder farmers. The evaluation also highlights the importance of knowledge exchange, peer-to-peer learning, and collaboration in fostering innovation and addressing shared agricultural challenges. Implications of these findings suggest that SSTC initiatives have the potential to contribute significantly to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 2, and that continued support and coordination are necessary to sustain momentum and ensure long-term impact.

The evaluation objective of the South-South and Triangular Cooperation (SSTC) initiative was to assess its effectiveness in advancing food security and nutrition national agendas in participating countries. The methodology involved a series of panel discussions, workshops, and capacity-building training programs, which brought together government representatives, international organizations, and local stakeholders to share knowledge, experiences, and best practices. Key findings indicate that SSTC has created synergies that benefit both education and local agriculture, ultimately strengthening national capacities and driving sustainable development across the Global South. The initiative has also facilitated the exchange of best practices and sharing of experiences between countries, leveraging SSTC to improve social protection systems, enhance governance mechanisms, and support vulnerable populations. Implications of the SSTC initiative suggest that continued collaboration and knowledge exchange between participating countries and international organizations will be essential to further enhance food supplementation governance processes, promote sustainability, and increase reach and coverage of social protection programs.

This evaluation aimed to assess the effectiveness of South-South and Triangular Cooperation (SSTC) in achieving the 2030 Agenda's Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 2 and SDG 17. The evaluation employed a qualitative methodology, analyzing data from WFP's Annual Country Reports (ACRs) and other sources to assess the impact of SSTC on national institutions, resource mobilization, and sustainable partnerships. Key findings indicate that SSTC has contributed to the transformation of international cooperation norms and principles, with national institutions taking a central stage as main actors in SSTC. In 2024, 85 national institutions provided technical and/or financial resources to WFP-facilitated SSTC, largely thanks to Centers of Excellence in Brazil, China, and Côte d'Ivoire. This has fostered national ownership, resource mobilization, and sustainable partnerships, resulting in tangible outcomes towards SDG 2 and SDG 17. The evaluation also highlights the consolidation of WFP's offer in areas such as school feeding, social protection, nutrition, and smallholder farmers market support. Implications of these findings suggest that SSTC can support timely and effective disaster response, and that WFP's engagement in SSTC has positioned it as a partner of choice for host governments.

This evaluation aimed to assess the impact of livelihood programmes on household resilience, with a focus on food security, agricultural production, and access to education and health facilities. The evaluation employed a randomized controlled trial (RCT) design, comparing households in newly eligible villages randomly assigned to three arms: unconditional cash or food transfers (UCTs), food or cash transfers for work on assets (FFA), and a comparison group that did not receive UCTs or FFA. The evaluation collected data through high-frequency surveys (bimonthly surveys following the baseline) and a qualitative component to cross-check conclusions and identify programme-related issues. Key findings indicate that access to FFA or transfers resulted in fewer households being severely food insecure, while there was an increase in the share of households experiencing moderate or no food insecurity. The evaluation also found that different types of households benefit differently from the programme, with implications for targeting and programming. The co-location of livelihoods, nutrition, and health interventions did not lead to additional improvements that are statistically significant in the short run. The evaluation's findings have implications for programme design, targeting, and implementation, and can inform strategies to improve household resilience and food security.

This evaluation aimed to assess the impact of floods and other factors on agricultural production in the Lao People's Democratic Republic. The study employed a mixed-methods approach, combining household surveys, focus group discussions, and review of existing datasets to estimate annual crop area, yield, and production. Key findings indicate that while floods had a severe impact on crops at the local level, their overall effect on national paddy and vegetable production remained limited. Paddy yields declined over the past decade, primarily due to inadequate access to and application of critical agricultural inputs, such as fertilizers and improved certified seeds. In 2024, paddy yields were estimated to be moderately below the five-year average, and paddy production was estimated at 3.8 million tonnes, about 3 percent above the previous five-year average. The agricultural sector contributed 13 percent to the country's total GDP in 2023 and employed more than 60 percent of the workforce. However, the sector is inadequately funded, with an Agriculture Orientation Index estimated at a low of 0.28 in 2022. The study highlights the need for increased investment in agriculture to improve productivity and address the challenges faced by farming households, including high food and fuel prices, limited availability of agricultural inputs, and the impact of natural hazards and poor harvests.

This evaluation aimed to assess the effectiveness of the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and the World Food Programme (WFP) Country Strategic Analysis and Monitoring (CFSAM) to Sri Lanka. The evaluation employed a comprehensive methodology, analyzing various reports and documents related to the CFSAM, including its objectives, implementation, and outcomes. Key findings indicate that the CFSAM has been instrumental in providing strategic guidance and support to the Government of Sri Lanka in addressing food security and nutrition challenges. The CFSAM has also facilitated the mobilization of international support and resources, contributing to the country's progress in achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The evaluation highlights the importance of continued collaboration between the FAO, WFP, and the Government of Sri Lanka to sustain the momentum and ensure the long-term impact of the CFSAM. The implications of this evaluation are that the CFSAM should be continued and strengthened to address emerging challenges and opportunities in the country's food security and nutrition landscape.

This formative strategic evaluation assessed how the World Food Programme (WFP) has addressed its commitments to protection from sexual exploitation and abuse (PSEA), with the objective of evaluating the effectiveness of WFP's PSEA approach and identifying areas for improvement. The evaluation methodology involved extensive consultation and reflection with internal and external stakeholders, as well as an analysis of WFP's policies, procedures, and practices related to PSEA. Key findings of the evaluation include: 

WFP has made notable contributions to inter-agency PSEA activity, including the development of an inter-agency capacity assessment tool and strategic partnerships with other organizations. However, there is a lack of clarity among staff on how to address PSEA, particularly in the context of WFP's increasing adoption of a more "enabling" role with governments. 

The evaluation also found that WFP's PSEA system is not yet fully effective, with limited communication on progress being made to improve investigation systems and mechanisms, and a lack of systematic approach to identify and prioritize limited PSEA capacity support from headquarters or regional bureaux. 

The evaluation recommends that WFP should: articulate a detailed definition of zero tolerance on inaction on PSEA and what is expected of all staff; describe how WFP will fulfill the core IASC commitments for 2022-2026 on PSEA, emphasizing those on prevention; formalize the minimum required PSEA architecture at the headquarters, regional, and country levels; and provide guidance on how resources and victim support will be provided. 

The implications of these findings and recommendations are that WFP needs to prioritize the effective mainstreaming of PSEA commitments, including planning, resourcing, monitoring, and reporting to managers and senior levels of WFP. This will require a sustained effort to build trust among internal and external stakeholders and to develop the necessary capacity and resources to support PSEA efforts.

This evaluation aimed to assess the continued relevance of the World Food Programme's (WFP) policies on HIV/AIDS and nutrition, and the effects achieved as a result of those policies. The evaluation also aimed to assess the extent to which WFP has sufficient organizational readiness to meet the challenges set out in the Decade of Action on Nutrition (2016-2025) and in corporate guiding frameworks. The evaluation employed a global scope, examining WFP's policies on nutrition and HIV/AIDS, as well as recent developments in nutrition-related programming. The evaluation also looked at a purposefully selected number of countries representing the wide spectrum of activities being carried out and supported by WFP in nutrition, including HIV/AIDS. Key findings included the continued relevance of WFP's policies on HIV/AIDS and nutrition, but with a need for refinement to bring them up to date with current priorities and evidence. The evaluation also found that WFP's effectiveness is increased through working in partnership, and that working in partnerships has the potential to contribute to improved outcomes, systems change, and sustainability. Furthermore, the evaluation highlighted the importance of WFP's role in supporting all nutritionally vulnerable population groups, including a clear articulation of the approach to HIV/AIDS-sensitive programming. The implications of these findings are that WFP should continue to prioritize nutrition and HIV/AIDS programming, and that partnerships should be strengthened to achieve improved outcomes and sustainability.

This evaluation aimed to develop a Strategic Roadmap to support the advancement of SUN Business Networks (SBNs) in the Asia region, with the overall objective of increasing engagement of the private sector in nutrition. The methodology involved stakeholder consultations, analysis of regional trends, and mapping of regional stakeholders. Key findings included the need for a regional platform to facilitate implementation of the Roadmap and support national SBNs, as well as the identification of six priority areas of engagement: food quality and safety, rice/wheat fortification, and technical assistance to small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). The evaluation also highlighted the importance of cross-country knowledge sharing and the need to strengthen the capacity of national SBNs through better knowledge sharing, learning, and enhancing of technical expertise. The implications of these findings are that a Regional SBN Platform should be established to support national SBNs, with a focus on strengthening capacity, increasing technical expertise and financial resources, forging multi-sectoral coalitions and alliances, and implementing highly effective multi-sectoral solutions. The evaluation recommends the establishment of an informal Regional SBN Advisory Council/Board to effectively engage regional businesses and other regional stakeholders, and the development of a presentation with an overview of SBN in the Asia Pacific and strategic engagement areas requiring private sector support.

This evaluation aims to assess the relevance and appropriateness of the World Food Programme's (WFP) approaches to targeting and prioritization for direct food/cash assistance interventions, as well as their effects on food security and nutrition status of targeted communities. To achieve this objective, the evaluation will employ a mixed-methods approach, combining desk-based analysis, case studies of six countries, and stakeholder engagement. The evaluation will draw on a range of data sources, including primary and secondary data, and will adhere to the 2020 UN Evaluation Group (UNEG) ethical guidelines to ensure impartiality, cultural sensitivity, and protection of participants' rights. The evaluation is expected to provide insights into the effectiveness of WFP's targeting and prioritization practices, identify areas for improvement, and inform the way forward for the organization.
